prompt: Evaluate this relativist line of reasoning about medical autonomy: 1. Whether a person is seen as a bearer of inviolable individual rights or as a node in a family or community system is determined by deep cultural narratives and institutions. 2. These narratives also determine what counts as "harm" in medicine: in some societies, letting an adult refuse life-saving care is the worst harm; in others, overriding their refusal is the worst harm. 3. There is no culture-independent moral court of appeal that can declare one conception of medical harm uniquely correct without presupposing one culture’s narratives. Suppose a hospital in Society X routinely sedates and operates on competent pregnant women without their informed consent, believing that protecting the fetus and the family’s honor trumps the woman’s autonomy. International critics call this a gross, objectively wrongful violation of human rights. If premises (1)–(3) are true, does the accusation of a "gross, objectively wrongful violation" report an objective moral fact about Society X, or only express the critics’ local standards with no universal authority over Society X? Give your considered conclusion directly, indicating whether you think there is any stance-independent wrong here.
